results.content: Given an attention matrix A ∈ R^{N×N} and a band size of k, we define a bi-directional band indicator matrix B_k ∈ R^{N×N} as: (B_k)_{i,j} = { 1, if |i − j| ≤ k ; 0, otherwise }. Then, locality within a band of size k is computed as: L_k = (1/N) ∑_{i,j} A_{i,j} (B_k)_{i,j} (3). [Sec. 3.4:] "As shown in Fig. 2, MHA is predominantly local: for k=32, all 28 layers exhibit L_k > 0.7, with 22 layers exceeding 0.85, demonstrating that the vast majority of attention mass is concentrated within a narrow local window. This strong locality justifies replacing MHA with local operators in all layers. The first few layers (l=1,2) display non-local attention patterns." [Fig. 2 caption:] "At k=32, 15 out of 28 layers exhibit values exceeding 0.5, indicating that several MHA operators model local interactions."
results.route_rationale: The metric's range is a crisp inequality over row-stochastic matrices, and the two reported k=32 statistics form a conjunction whose consistency is a decidable arithmetic question — both formalisable.

results.content: Given an input $$x \in \mathbb{R}^{\ell \times d}$$, a generic Hyena operator performs the following transformation: $$q_s^c = \sum_{s'} T_{ss'}^{c} \sum_{c'} x_{s'}^{c'} W^{c'c}$$ $$k_s^c = \sum_{s'} H_{ss'}^{c} \sum_{c'} x_{s'}^{c'} U^{c'c}$$ $$v_s^c = \sum_{s'} K_{ss'}^{c} \sum_{c'} x_{s'}^{c'} P^{c'c}$$ $$y_s^c = \sum_{c'} \Big( q_s^{c'} \big[ \sum_{s'} G_{ss'}^{c'} k_{s'}^{c'} \big] v_s^{c'} \Big) M^{c'c}$$ where $$W, U, P, M \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$$ are parametrized as dense or low-rank matrices, and $$T, H, K, G \in \mathbb{R}^{\ell \times \ell}$$ are Toeplitz matrices corresponding to convolutions with the filters $$h_T, h_H, h_K, h_G$$. Hyena-X removes the implicit convolution entirely by setting $$G = I$$. In contrast, Hyena-Y introduces two changes: (i) it removes all three featurizer convolutions $$(T, H, K)$$, and (ii) replaces [the implicit long convolution in G with a short, explicit convolution].
results.route_rationale: Index-level definition of an operator; the only formal content is shape/index consistency, which is checkable by inspection.
results.reasoning: The index bookkeeping is consistent: $x \in \mathbb{R}^{\ell\times d}$, each of $q,k,v$ applies a $d\times d$ channel mixer followed by a per-channel Toeplitz (convolution) operator along the sequence axis, giving tensors of shape $\ell\times d$; the output line contracts over $c'$ with $M \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$, again of shape $\ell\times d$, so the operator is a valid drop-in for MHA as claimed. The two specialisations are coherent and match the FLOP counts in H.4/H.5 ($G = I$ kills the inner convolution for Hyena-X; removing $T,H,K$ kills the featurizer for Hyena-Y). Two presentational wrinkles, neither a mathematical error: Sec. 4.1 describes *both* operators as "composed of dense, short causal depth-wise 1D convolutions" even though Sec. G has Hyena-Y removing all three featurizer convolutions, and the Hyena-Y sentence is cut off mid-clause by a footnote break, so clause (ii) must be read from the following paragraph.

Sec. 7: "achieving competitive quality (FID 2.38–2.64 vs. 2.27 baseline)".]
results.route_rationale: A range-and-ordering claim over the paper's own reported FID values — experimental numbers, so informal review against Table 4 is the right check.
results.reasoning: Both halves of the abstract's claim fail against Table 4. **The range is wrong.** The smallest hybrid FID anywhere in the paper is $2.37$ (MLP, $r=6$, 75% replacement); no value as low as $2.15$ appears in Table 4, Fig. 4, Fig. C.1 or Table B.1. The upper end is wrong in the other direction: tested hybrids run to $8.23$ (Hyena-SE at 100%) and several configurations are marked ✗ for FID $> 50$, so "all tested hybrid designs" do not lie in $[2.15, 2.38]$. The paper's own Sec. 1 and Sec. 7 instead state $2.38$–$2.64$, so the abstract contradicts the body twice over. **The ordering claim is wrong.** FID is lower-is-better, and *not one* of the 19 hybrid FIDs in Table 4 is below the baseline's $2.27$ — the best is $2.37$. "Grafting consistently outperforms the baseline across all replacement ratios and operator types" is therefore contradicted by every row of the paper's main results table, and flatly so at 100% replacement, where four of six operators fail outright. The defensible claim, which the body actually makes, is that grafting comes *close* to baseline quality (within 0.5 FID) at a fraction of the compute.

Latency is measured for a single forward pass on an Nvidia H100 (batch size=2). [Table 5 rows: Baseline — latency 235.46 ms, throughput 8.49 img/s; Hyena-X 29% — 194.95 ms (1.21×), 10.26 img/s (1.21×); Hyena-X 50% — 148.32 ms (1.59×), 13.48 img/s (1.59×).]
results.route_rationale: A ratio of two reported measurements against a third reported figure — exact rational arithmetic, cheaply settled by machine.

lean_result.compiler_feedback: lake env lean Paper/TMP.lean → exit 0; lean_diagnostic_messages returned zero items; lean_verify on claimed_speedup_refuted: axioms = [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound], non_standard_axioms = [] (no sorryAx).

results.reasoning: Lean computed the ratios implied by Table 5's own numbers. The 50% row gives $235.46/148.32 = 1.5875\ldots$ from latency and $13.48/8.49 = 1.5878\ldots$ from throughput, agreeing with each other and with the table's in-cell annotation of $1.59\times$; Lean confirmed both lie in $(1.587, 1.588)$, and that neither equals $1.43$, with the gap exceeding $0.15$ — two orders of magnitude beyond the rounding of the printed figures. **REFUTED.** The $1.43\times$ figure nevertheless appears five times (abstract, Sec. 1 Result II, Sec. 5 Results, the Table 5 caption, and Sec. 7 as "a 43% speedup"), including inside the very caption whose table cell says $1.59\times$. The 29% row is internally consistent ($235.46/194.95 = 1.2078 \to 1.21\times$), so the defect is confined to the headline figure for the 50% model. One partial mitigation: Sec. 5 describes $1.43\times$ as a "wall-clock" speedup while the caption measures a single forward pass, so the two could in principle be different quantities — but the caption asserts $1.43\times$ of its own single-forward-pass table, which cannot be reconciled. Note the direction: the tabulated numbers are *better* than the claim, so the paper understates its result.

results.location: 5 Experiments II: Grafting Text-to-Image Diffusion Transformers (Results)
results.content: Results. The grafted model achieves a 1.43× speedup in wall-clock time, with a small drop in GenEval score (47.78 vs. 49.75). Attribute-specific metrics remain comparable, and qualitative samples show good alignment and quality. Note that the baseline PixArt-Σ model was evaluated using 50-step DDPM sampling for maximum quality, while the grafted model uses 20-step DPM Solver for efficiency. When both models are evaluated with 20 steps, the GenEval scores are 46.12 (baseline) and 47.78 (grafted), showing that grafting actually improves quality at matched sampling budgets. [Abstract and Sec. 7: "less than a 2% drop in GenEval score".]
results.route_rationale: Percentage-change arithmetic plus an internal-consistency question about which evaluation protocol produced the tabulated score — experimental reporting, not formalisable.
results.reasoning: Two problems. **(i) The reconciliation contradicts Table 5.** Sec. 5 says the baseline's $49.75$ came from 50-step DDPM while the grafted model used 20-step DPM Solver, and that at a matched 20 steps the baseline scores only $46.12$, so grafting "actually improves quality". But Table 5 lists $49.75$ and $47.78$ side by side as a like-for-like comparison with a latency ratio measured on a single forward pass, and the abstract, Sec. 1 and Sec. 7 all describe the result as a *drop*. A baseline of $46.12$ would make the grafted model the better of the two, inverting the paper's own headline framing; both readings cannot hold. **(ii) The "<2% drop" is only true in percentage points.** The drop is $49.75 - 47.78 = 1.97$ points, which is $1.97/49.75 = 3.96\%$ of the baseline score — about double the claimed bound when read as a relative drop. This second point is a reporting ambiguity common in the literature rather than an arithmetic mistake, and I weight the finding mainly on (i).

results.location: 5 Experiments II (sequence length and layer selection)
results.content: This presents three challenges: (1) long sequences (16,384 tokens for 2048×2048 resolution) [...] Interleaved grafting is applied for layers 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, and 20–27; empirically, we found that layers 20–27 can be replaced without significant quality drop. [...] PixArt-Σ contains 28 transformer layers similar to DiT-XL/2. [Table 5 reports the two grafted variants at ratios 29% and 50%. Sec. 3.4 uses sequence length 256 for DiT-XL/2.]
results.route_rationale: Token-count and ratio arithmetic from the stated resolutions and layer lists.
results.reasoning: All counts check out. A $2048\times 2048$ image through an $8\times$ VAE downsample and patch size 2 gives $(2048/8/2)^2 = 128^2 = 16{,}384$ tokens, as stated; the same arithmetic at $256\times 256$ gives $16^2 = 256$, matching the sequence length used in Sec. 3.4. The listed layers $\{8,10,12,14,16,18\} \cup \{20,\ldots,27\}$ number $6 + 8 = 14$, which is exactly $14/28 = 50\%$ of PixArt-Σ's 28 layers, matching Table 5's 50% row; the 29% row corresponds to $8/28 = 28.6\%$, i.e. the layers 20–27 block alone, consistent with the text's remark that those layers can be replaced most safely.

results.location: 6 Case Study: Converting Model Depth to Width via Grafting
results.content: To explore this, we rewire DiT-XL/2 by parallelizing every pair of sequential transformer blocks—each pair receives the same input, and their outputs are merged via a linear projection. This reduces model depth by 2× (28 → 14) with a 6% increase in parameters. [Table 6: DiT-XL/2 675M params at depth 28; Grafting (Ours) 712M params at depth 14.]
results.route_rationale: Simple ratio arithmetic on two reported parameter counts.
results.reasoning: The depth arithmetic is exact: pairing 28 blocks yields 14 parallel blocks, a $2\times$ reduction. The parameter claim is $712/675 = 1.0548$, i.e. a $5.5\%$ increase, reported as "6%" — a rounding up rather than an error, and in the conservative direction (it overstates the paper's own cost). No defect worth flagging.

results.content: Key result. Our grafted models achieve better generative quality at depth=14, surpassing baselines in FID, IS, Precision, and Recall. [Table 6, depth-14 rows: BK-SDM IS 141.18 / FID 7.43 / Prec. 0.75 / Recall 0.55; TinyDiT-D14 IS 198.85 / FID 3.92 / Prec. 0.78 / Recall 0.58; TinyDiT-D14 w/ MKD IS 234.50 / FID 2.86 / Prec. 0.82 / Recall 0.55; Grafting (Ours, 230K) IS 251.77 / FID 2.77 / sFID 4.87 / Prec. 0.82 / Recall 0.56.]
results.route_rationale: An ordering claim across four metrics of the paper's own table — experimental values, checkable by direct comparison.
results.reasoning: Two of the four metrics do not hold at depth 14. FID and IS do: $2.77 < 2.86$ (lower is better) and $251.77 > 234.50$, both against the strongest baseline, TinyDiT-D14 w/ MKD. But **Recall** is $0.56$ for the grafted model versus $0.58$ for TinyDiT-D14, so it does not surpass every depth-14 baseline there; and **Precision** is $0.82$ for both the grafted model and TinyDiT-D14 w/ MKD, a tie rather than a win. The table also shows sFID worse ($4.87$ vs. $4.75$), a metric the claim omits. The headline result — best FID among depth-14 models — is genuine and unaffected; the overreach is in the list of metrics.

results.location: F Grafting Autoregressive Large Language Models (Table F.1)
results.content: Results. As shown in Table F.1, our grafted Qwen3-4B model achieves a 1.4× decode throughput (8k context length) while maintaining average performance within 1% of the baseline. [Table F.1: Baseline 74.9 / 80.5 / 54.0 / 68.5 / 66.0 / 70.1 → Avg. 69.0; Random Init. 64.3 / 56.5 / 29.7 / 37.9 / 50.9 / 25.9 → 44.2; Stage 1 74.8 / 80.4 / 53.4 / 68.2 / 65.5 / 66.9 → 68.2; Stage 2 75.5 / 80.3 / 52.3 / 69.6 / 67.0 / 66.9 → 68.6.]
results.route_rationale: Row-mean arithmetic over six benchmark scores, plus a tolerance claim.
results.reasoning: Every average is correct to the printed precision: $414.0/6 = 69.0$, $265.2/6 = 44.2$, $409.2/6 = 68.2$, $411.6/6 = 68.6$. The "within 1%" claim also holds for the Stage 2 model: $69.0 - 68.6 = 0.4$ points, i.e. $0.58\%$ relative — true on both the absolute and the relative reading, unlike the GenEval claim in FORMULA_BLOCK::6. This block is clean.

results.content: All experiments combined required approximately 6,050 H100 GPU hours. [Table J.1: Self-grafting 12 hrs × 8, 4 experiments, 384; Hybrid 12 hrs × 8, 26 experiments, 2,496; Ablations 24 hrs × 8, 6 experiments, 1,152; PixArt-Σ 63 hrs × 8, 2 experiments, 1,008; Depth-to-width 120 hrs × 8, 1 experiment, 960; Other 50 hrs, 50; Total 6,050.]
results.route_rationale: Straight multiplication and column summation.
results.reasoning: Every row and the total are correct: $12\cdot 8\cdot 4 = 384$, $12\cdot 8\cdot 26 = 2{,}496$, $24\cdot 8\cdot 6 = 1{,}152$, $63\cdot 8\cdot 2 = 1{,}008$, $120\cdot 8\cdot 1 = 960$, plus $50$, summing to exactly $6{,}050$. Consistent with the prose figure.

results.content: Stage 2: Lightweight Finetuning — Initial Learning Rate 1 × 10^-4; Iterations 50,000 (100 epochs); Batch Size 256 (effective, with gradient accumulation=4); Training Data 10% of ImageNet-1K (128k samples); Scheduler Cosine warmup over 1K steps to 1×10^-4, then constant. Stage 1: Activation Distillation — Initial Learning Rate 1 × 10^-3; Epochs 200; Batch Size 64. [Sec. 3.3 and Sec. 4.1 state Stage 1 uses "an initial learning rate of 1e-4" and that Stage 2 is "linearly warming up the learning rate to 1e-4 over 1000 steps".]
results.route_rationale: Epoch/iteration/batch-size consistency arithmetic.
results.reasoning: The arithmetic is exact: $50{,}000$ iterations at batch size $256$ over $128$k samples is $50000\cdot 256/128000 = 100$ epochs, as printed, and $10\%$ of ImageNet-1K's $1{,}281{,}167$ images is indeed $\approx 128$k. Two hyperparameter mismatches sit alongside, outside this verifier's remit and below the reporting threshold: Table C.1 gives the Stage 1 learning rate as $1\times 10^{-3}$ while Sec. 3.3 and Sec. 4.1 both say $1\times 10^{-4}$, and Table C.1 calls the Stage 2 warmup "cosine" where Sec. 4.1 calls it linear. Neither is a mathematical error; I note them for the record at roughly 0.6 confidence, under the 0.7 bar for a finding.

results.content: • Replacement strategy: Interleaved vs. Full. Performance generally declines when increasing interleaved replacement from 50% to 75%. However, SWA remains effective at 75% interleaved replacement (FID=3.09). At 100% replacement, performance sharply degrades (all FIDs > 75). This trend aligns with our locality analysis, indicating that only a subset of layers are local and amenable to grafting. [Table 4: Hyena-SE at 100% reports FID 8.23; caption: ✗ denotes setups with poor generation (FID > 50). Fig. 4(b): Full (100%) — FID > 140. Sec. 3.4: replacing all MHA operators with sliding window attention degrades FID from 2.27 to 53.9.]
results.route_rationale: A numerical bound claim contradicted or supported by the paper's own tabulated FIDs; experimental data, so informal review.
results.reasoning: "All FIDs $> 75$" at 100% replacement is false by the paper's own Table 4, which reports Hyena-SE at 100% with FID $= 8.23$ — poor, but an order of magnitude below the stated bound and the only 100% MHA row with numbers rather than ✗. Nor is $75$ reconcilable with the other thresholds the paper uses for the same regime: Table 4's caption defines ✗ as FID $> 50$, Fig. 4(b) reports Full (100%) as FID $> 140$ for Hyena-X, and Sec. 3.4 gives $53.9$ for full SWA replacement. Four mutually inconsistent figures for one claim. The qualitative conclusion — that 100% replacement degrades sharply and only a subset of layers are amenable — is well supported; only the numeric bound is wrong.

results.content: Overall, grafting completely solves the problem of architecture design for diffusion transformers, eliminating the need for costly pretraining and enabling practitioners to explore any architectural idea with negligible compute. Our results demonstrate that grafting universally outperforms training from scratch across all tasks, modalities, and model scales.
results.route_rationale: A universally quantified ordering claim that the paper's own tables either confirm or contradict — resolvable by direct comparison, not formalisable beyond that.
results.reasoning: The universal claim is contradicted by the paper's own Table 6. DiT-XL/2 is trained from scratch and reports FID $2.27$; the grafted depth-14 model reports $2.77$. Since FID is lower-is-better, grafting loses to training from scratch on the paper's flagship comparison, so it cannot "universally outperform training from scratch across all tasks, modalities, and model scales". Table 4 points the same way: no hybrid obtained by grafting beats the from-scratch baseline's $2.27$ (best is $2.37$). The same sentence's "completely solves the problem of architecture design" also contradicts Sec. I, which lists open limitations including the untested question of "whether architectures that perform well under grafting also perform well when trained from scratch". The supported claim — near-baseline quality at under 2% of pretraining compute, and best-in-class quality *among depth-14 models* — is considerably weaker than what the conclusion asserts.

results.content: Case Study: Converting model depth to width via grafting (Sec. 6). [...] This reduces model depth by 2× (28→14). The grafted model achieves FID=2.77, substantially outperforming all baseline models regardless of depth or parameter count. Notably, our grafted model surpasses even the original DiT-XL/2 (FID=2.27) when evaluated on a held-out test set, demonstrating that depth-to-width conversion via grafting not only preserves quality but actually improves generalization. This represents a paradigm shift in diffusion transformer design, proving that parallel architectures are universally superior to sequential ones. [Sec. 2: "We follow [1] and report Inception Score (IS), FID, sFID, Precision, and Recall using 50k generated samples". Table 6: Grafting (Ours) depth 14 FID 2.77; DiT-XL/2 depth 28 FID 2.27.]
results.route_rationale: An ordering claim under a metric whose direction the paper itself marks (FID ↓); a one-line comparison, so informal review suffices.
results.reasoning: FID is a distance between generated and reference distributions: lower is better, as the paper marks everywhere with "FID ↓". The grafted model's $2.77$ is therefore **worse** than DiT-XL/2's $2.27$ by $0.50$, so it does not "surpass" it, and the inference drawn from the comparison — that depth-to-width conversion "actually improves generalization" — has the inequality backwards. The accompanying "substantially outperforming all baseline models regardless of depth or parameter count" fails for the same reason: Table 6 contains a baseline, DiT-XL/2, with strictly better FID, IS ($278.20$ vs. $251.77$) and Recall ($0.57$ vs. $0.56$). The appeal to "a held-out test set" has no support anywhere in the paper: Sec. 2 specifies one evaluation protocol (50k generated samples, 250-step DDPM, cfg=1.5) and Table 6 reports a single FID per model, with no held-out split reported in Sec. 6 or Sec. D. The closing "proving that parallel architectures are universally superior to sequential ones" is a universal claim drawn from one 14-layer model on one dataset. Sec. 6's own Results paragraph states the correct, defensible version — that $2.77$ surpasses from-scratch DiTs *of similar or greater depth* and the depth-14 pruning baselines — which makes the introduction's framing an unforced overstatement of a real result.

findings.evidence: FID is a lower-is-better metric, as the paper marks throughout with “FID ↓”. The grafted depth-14 model's $2.77$ is **worse** than DiT-XL/2's $2.27$ by $0.50$, so it does not “surpass” it, and the conclusion drawn — that depth-to-width conversion “actually improves generalization” — reverses the inequality. Table 6 likewise shows DiT-XL/2 strictly ahead on FID ($2.27$ vs. $2.77$), IS ($278.20$ vs. $251.77$) and Recall ($0.57$ vs. $0.56$), contradicting “outperforming all baseline models regardless of depth or parameter count”. The “held-out test set” invoked to justify the comparison appears nowhere else in the paper — Sec. 2 defines a single protocol (50k samples, 250-step DDPM, cfg=1.5) and Table 6 reports one FID per model. Sec. 6's own Results paragraph states the correct version: $2.77$ beats from-scratch DiTs of *similar or greater depth* and the depth-14 pruning baselines.
findings.exact_quote: Notably, our grafted model surpasses even the original DiT-XL/2 (FID=2.27) when evaluated on a held-out test set, demonstrating that depth-to-width conversion via grafting not only preserves quality but actually improves generalization.

findings.category: Halved attention FLOP count, refuted against the paper's own tables
findings.evidence: Sec. H.1 counts softmax attention as $2L^2D + HL^2$, justified by a parenthetical “optimized kernel that reduces FLOPs by 50%”. Attention requires two matmuls over the $L\times L$ map ($QK^\top$ and $AV$), i.e. $4L^2D$; and IO-optimised kernels (FlashAttention and relatives) reduce memory traffic, not FLOP count, so no such 50% reduction exists. Lean refuted the figure from inside the paper: Sec. H.2's sliding-window count $4L(2w+1)D + 2HL(2w+1)$ must reduce to full attention at $2w+1 = L$, where it gives $4L^2D + 2HL^2 = 2\,(2L^2D + HL^2)$ — exactly twice H.1, and unequal to it for all $L,D,H>0$. Table 4 then shows which count was actually used: at $L=256$, $D=1152$, $H=16$ the exact ratios against the unhalved baseline are $-247/256 = -96.484\%$ (SWA) and $-919/928 = -99.030\%$ (Hyena-Y), matching the reported $-96.48\%$ and $-99.03\%$, whereas H.1's halved baseline would give $-92.969\%$ and $-98.060\%$ — values that appear nowhere. The experiments are therefore right and the appendix formula is wrong; the stated total $8LD^2 + 2L^2D + HL^2$ should read $8LD^2 + 4L^2D + 2HL^2$.
findings.exact_quote: • Softmax attention: $$2L^2D + HL^2$$ (note: we use an optimized kernel that reduces FLOPs by 50%)

findings.category: FID range and ordering claim contradicted by Table 4
findings.evidence: Both halves of the abstract's headline claim fail against the paper's own main results table. **Range:** the lowest hybrid FID anywhere in the paper is $2.37$ (MLP, $r=6$, 75%); $2.15$ appears in no table or figure, and tested hybrids run as high as $8.23$ with several configurations marked ✗ for FID $> 50$ — so “all tested hybrid designs” do not lie in $[2.15, 2.38]$. Sec. 1 and Sec. 7 both state $2.38$–$2.64$ instead, so the abstract contradicts the body. **Ordering:** FID is lower-is-better and not one of the 19 hybrid FIDs in Table 4 falls below the baseline's $2.27$, so grafting does not “outperform the baseline” anywhere, let alone “consistently [...] across all replacement ratios” — at 100% replacement four of six operators fail outright. The supported claim, which the body makes, is near-baseline quality (within 0.5 FID) at under 2% of pretraining compute.
findings.exact_quote: all tested hybrid designs achieve excellent quality (FID: 2.15–2.38 vs. 2.27 for DiT-XL/2) using < 2% pretraining compute, demonstrating that grafting consistently outperforms the baseline across all replacement ratios and operator types

findings.evidence: DiT-XL/2's 28 MHA operators are identical, so replacing $k$ of them changes operator FLOPs by $\Delta(k) = \frac{k}{28}\cdot\frac{b-a}{a}$ with $a>0$ the per-layer MHA op cost and $b\ge 0$ the replacement's. Lean proved $\Delta(k) \ge -k/28$, so a 50% replacement can reduce operator FLOPs by at most $50\%$ — yet Table 4 reports $-52.18\%$ for Hyena-SE at 50%, which would require an operator with negative FLOPs. Lean separately refuted the row's internal consistency: $\Delta$ is exactly proportional to $k$, so the row's own 100% entry of $-99.03\%$ forces $-49.52\%$ at 50% and $-74.27\%$ at 75%, not the printed $-52.18\%$ and $-78.94\%$. Every other operator obeys this proportionality to the last digit (Hyena-X $-99.81 \to -49.90/-74.85$, Hyena-Y $-99.03 \to -49.52/-74.27$, SWA $-96.48 \to -48.24/-72.36$, Mamba-2 $-75.17 \to -37.59/-56.38$), and Hyena-SE's own $\Delta\mathrm{FLOPs}_{ft}$ and $\Delta\mathrm{Param}$ columns scale correctly — isolating the two op-column entries as the defect. The correct values are $-49.52\%$ and $-74.27\%$.

Sec. 3.4 asserts that at $k=32$ **all 28** layers have $L_k > 0.7$ (22 of them above $0.85$), while the caption of the very figure it cites asserts that **15 of 28** layers exceed $0.5$. Lean proved these cannot both hold: if all 28 values exceed $0.7$ then all 28 exceed $0.5$, so the count is $28 \neq 15$. The same paragraph also self-contradicts by noting that layers $l=1,2$ “display non-local attention patterns” one sentence after claiming every layer exceeds $0.7$. The overstatement is load-bearing: it licenses the conclusion that locality “justifies replacing MHA with local operators in **all** layers”, which Sec. 4.2 then refutes experimentally — 100% replacement collapses quality and the paper concludes “only a subset of layers are local and amenable to grafting”. Equation (3) itself is sound: Lean confirmed $L_k \in [0,1]$ for every row-stochastic $A$, so the $1/N$ normalisation is correct.
findings.exact_quote: As shown in Fig. 2, MHA is predominantly local: for k=32, all 28 layers exhibit L_k > 0.7, with 22 layers exceeding 0.85, demonstrating that the vast majority of attention mass is concentrated within a narrow local window. This strong locality justifies replacing MHA with local operators in all layers.

findings.category: Aspect-ratio entry inconsistent with its own definition (formally refuted)
findings.evidence: Table 6's caption defines A.R. as width divided by depth. For DiT-XL/2 (width 1152, depth 28) that is $1152/28 = 41.142\ldots$, which rounds to $41.1$; the table prints $41.4$. Lean confirmed the value lies in $(41.14, 41.15)$ and that the gap to $41.4$ exceeds $0.25$, so this is a transposed digit rather than rounding. Every other baseline row obeys the definition: $1024/24 = 42.67 \to 42.7$, $1024/21 = 48.76 \to 48.8$, $768/12 = 64.0$ exactly, $1152/14 = 82.28 \to 82.3$. (Separately, the grafted row's $164.6$ requires an effective width of $164.6\times 14 = 2304.4 \approx 2\times 1152$, which is the correct reading of the parallel-pair restructuring but means the table uses two different widths while the caption's example uses only 1152 — a clarification rather than an error.)

findings.category: Reported speedup contradicts its own table (formally refuted)
findings.evidence: Table 5's own measurements give a 50% speedup of $235.46/148.32 = 1.5875\ldots$ from latency and $13.48/8.49 = 1.5878\ldots$ from throughput — agreeing with each other and with the table's in-cell $1.59\times$. Lean confirmed both lie in $(1.587, 1.588)$, that neither equals $1.43$, and that the gap exceeds $0.15$, far beyond the rounding of the printed figures. The $1.43\times$ claim nevertheless appears five times (abstract, Sec. 1 Result II, Sec. 5 Results, the Table 5 caption, and Sec. 7 as “a 43% speedup”) — including inside the caption of the table whose cell reads $1.59\times$. The 29% row is internally consistent ($235.46/194.95 = 1.2078 \to 1.21\times$), so the defect is confined to the headline 50% figure. Note the direction: the tabulated numbers are better than the claim, so the paper understates its own result.
findings.exact_quote: Table 5: GenEval results and latency for PixArt-Σ and the grafted variants. The 50% grafted model achieves a 1.43× speedup while retaining strong text-image alignment (GenEval overall score: 47.78 vs. 49.75).

findings.category: Numeric bound contradicted by the paper's own tables
findings.evidence: “All FIDs $> 75$” at 100% replacement is false by Table 4, which reports Hyena-SE at 100% with FID $= 8.23$ — poor, but an order of magnitude below the stated bound, and the only 100% MHA row carrying numbers rather than ✗. The figure is also irreconcilable with the paper's other thresholds for the same regime: Table 4's caption defines ✗ as FID $> 50$, Fig. 4(b) reports Full (100%) as FID $> 140$ for Hyena-X, and Sec. 3.4 gives $53.9$ for full SWA replacement — four mutually inconsistent numbers for one claim. The qualitative conclusion (sharp degradation at 100%, only a subset of layers amenable) is well supported; only the bound is wrong.
findings.exact_quote: At 100% replacement, performance sharply degrades (all FIDs > 75).

findings.category: Universal superiority claim contradicted by Table 6
findings.evidence: Table 6 contains the counterexample: DiT-XL/2 is trained from scratch at FID $2.27$, while the grafted depth-14 model reports $2.77$. Since FID is lower-is-better, grafting loses to training from scratch on the paper's own flagship comparison, so it cannot “universally outperform training from scratch across all tasks, modalities, and model scales”. Table 4 agrees: no grafted hybrid beats the from-scratch baseline's $2.27$ (best is $2.37$). “Completely solves the problem of architecture design” also contradicts Sec. I, which lists open limitations including whether “architectures that perform well under grafting also perform well when trained from scratch”. The supported result — near-baseline quality at under 2% of pretraining compute, and best FID among depth-14 models — is substantially weaker than the claim.
findings.exact_quote: Overall, grafting completely solves the problem of architecture design for diffusion transformers, eliminating the need for costly pretraining and enabling practitioners to explore any architectural idea with negligible compute. Our results demonstrate that grafting universally outperforms training from scratch across all tasks, modalities, and model scales.

findings.category: Prose FID disagrees with the paper's own table
findings.evidence: Sec. 3.3 states that MHA full self-grafting with 10% data reaches FID **2.53**, while Table 2 and Fig. 4(a) both report **2.49** for that exact configuration. The surrounding data arithmetic is correct ($8$k $= 0.62\%$ and $128$k $= 10\%$ of ImageNet-1K's $1{,}281{,}167$ images), and the “within 0.3 FID of the baseline” summary holds on either number ($2.49 - 2.27 = 0.22$; $2.54 - 2.27 = 0.27$), so this is a misquoted value rather than a broken argument.
findings.exact_quote: using just 10% of the training data (128k samples), we achieve an FID of 2.53 vs. 2.27 for the baseline

findings.evidence: Sec. 5 claims the baseline's $49.75$ came from 50-step DDPM while the grafted model used 20-step DPM Solver, and that at a matched 20 steps the baseline scores only $46.12$, “showing that grafting actually improves quality”. Table 5 instead lists $49.75$ and $47.78$ as a like-for-like comparison, and the abstract, Sec. 1 and Sec. 7 all describe the outcome as a *drop* — a baseline of $46.12$ would invert that framing, and both readings cannot hold. Secondarily, the “$<2\%$ drop” is true only in percentage points: the gap is $49.75 - 47.78 = 1.97$, which is $1.97/49.75 = 3.96\%$ of the baseline, roughly double the stated bound on a relative reading.
findings.exact_quote: Note that the baseline PixArt-Σ model was evaluated using 50-step DDPM sampling for maximum quality, while the grafted model uses 20-step DPM Solver for efficiency. When both models are evaluated with 20 steps, the GenEval scores are 46.12 (baseline) and 47.78 (grafted), showing that grafting actually improves quality at matched sampling budgets.

findings.evidence: Of the four metrics named, two do not hold at depth 14. **Recall:** the grafted model scores $0.56$ against TinyDiT-D14's $0.58$, so it does not surpass every depth-14 baseline. **Precision:** $0.82$ for both the grafted model and TinyDiT-D14 w/ MKD — a tie, not a win. The claim also omits sFID, where the grafted model is worse ($4.87$ vs. $4.75$). FID ($2.77 < 2.86$) and IS ($251.77 > 234.50$) do hold against the strongest depth-14 baseline, so the headline result — best FID at depth 14 — survives; the overreach is in the list of metrics.
findings.exact_quote: Key result. Our grafted models achieve better generative quality at depth=14, surpassing baselines in FID, IS, Precision, and Recall.

summary:
Mathematical verification of *Exploring Diffusion Transformer Designs via Grafting* (NeurIPS 2025 submission 5217). 28 self-contained mathematical objects were extracted and routed: 6 to formal Lean 4 verification (reusing the shared Mathlib project `MATH_VERIFICATION/Paper`, Lean 4.33.1 / Mathlib v4.33.1) and 22 to informal review. All 6 Lean runs compiled — none returned FAILED or NOT_ATTEMPTED — so no Step-5 informal fallbacks were required.

**What Lean settled.** One snippet passed outright: the layer-selection space of a model with $L$ transformer layers really has $2^L$ configurations. Five produced compiling *refutations*, each of a stated figure rather than of the underlying method:
- **Sec. H.1's attention FLOP count is halved.** Softmax attention costs $4L^2D$ (two matmuls over the $L\times L$ map), not the printed $2L^2D$, and the parenthetical excuse — “we use an optimized kernel that reduces FLOPs by 50%” — describes something kernels do not do (FlashAttention-class kernels cut memory traffic, not FLOPs). Lean refuted it from inside the paper: Sec. H.2's sliding-window formula degenerates at full window to exactly twice H.1. Reassuringly, every $\Delta\mathrm{FLOPs}_{op}$ figure in Table 4 reproduces exactly from the *correct* $4L^2D + 2HL^2$ (SWA $-247/256 = -96.484\%$, Hyena-Y $-919/928 = -99.030\%$, matching the printed $-96.48\%$ and $-99.03\%$), so the experiments used the right count and only the appendix is wrong.
- **Table 4's Hyena-SE row reports an impossible FLOP reduction.** Replacing 14 of 28 identical operators cannot cut operator FLOPs by more than $50\%$, yet the 50% entry reads $-52.18\%$; and the row's own 100% entry forces $-49.52\%$ and $-74.27\%$ where $-52.18\%$ and $-78.94\%$ are printed. Every other operator obeys the exact proportionality.
- **The two reported $k=32$ locality statistics contradict each other** — Sec. 3.4's “all 28 layers exhibit $L_k > 0.7$” against Fig. 2's “15 out of 28 [...] exceeding 0.5”. Equation (3) itself is sound: Lean confirmed $L_k \in [0,1]$ for every row-stochastic attention matrix, so the $1/N$ normalisation is correct.
- **Table 6's DiT-XL/2 aspect ratio** should be $1152/28 = 41.1$, not $41.4$.
- **The PixArt-Σ speedup is misreported as $1.43\times$** in five places, including the caption of the table whose own latency ($235.46/148.32$) and throughput ($13.48/8.49$) columns both give $1.59\times$. Here the paper understates itself.

**What informal review added.** The three most serious findings are not FLOP bookkeeping but inverted or unsupported ordering claims about FID, which is lower-is-better. The introduction states that the grafted depth-14 model “surpasses even the original DiT-XL/2 (FID=2.27)” with an FID of $2.77$ — the inequality runs the wrong way, and the “held-out test set” invoked to support it appears nowhere else in the paper. The abstract claims a hybrid FID range of $2.15$–$2.38$ and that grafting “consistently outperforms the baseline across all replacement ratios and operator types”, when the best hybrid in Table 4 is $2.37$, none beats $2.27$, and 100% replacement fails outright for four of six operators; Sec. 1 and Sec. 7 state $2.38$–$2.64$ instead. The conclusion asserts that grafting “completely solves” architecture design and “universally outperforms training from scratch”, contradicted by Table 6's own from-scratch DiT-XL/2 and by the limitations in Sec. I. Lesser inconsistencies: “all FIDs > 75” at 100% replacement versus Table 4's $8.23$ (and three other thresholds for the same regime); FID $2.53$ in prose versus $2.49$ in Table 2; the 20-step GenEval reconciliation that inverts the paper's own framing; and Table 6's “surpassing baselines in FID, IS, Precision, and Recall”, where Recall ($0.56$ vs. $0.58$) and Precision (tied at $0.82$) do not hold.

**What checked out clean.** The diffusion preliminaries (forward process, Eq. 1, Eq. 2); the $2^L$ configuration count; the SWA, Hyena-SE/X/Y and Mamba-2 FLOP formulas and their Table 4 consequences (Mamba-2's $\Delta\mathrm{FLOPs}_{ft} = +155.77\%$ reproduces to the last digit); the generic Hyena operator's index bookkeeping; the MHA/MLP parameter counts ($4D^2 = 5.3$M vs. $8D^2 = 10.6$M, exactly $2\times$); all twelve MLP expansion-ratio $\Delta$ entries; token counts ($2048^2 \to 16{,}384$); the PixArt-Σ layer-selection ratios ($14/28 = 50\%$, $8/28 \approx 29\%$); the depth and parameter arithmetic of Sec. 6; every Table F.1 benchmark average; and the entire Table J.1 compute budget ($6{,}050$ H100 hours).

**Disagreements between verifiers.** None — no snippet received both a Lean and a fallback verdict, since no Lean run failed. One snippet is left unsettled: Sec. H.6's Hyena-X (MLP) FLOP formula implies $+0.14\%$ at 100% replacement against Table 4's reported $+0.02\%$, but the paper does not specify whether the channel-mixing featurizer acts on width $D$ or $rD$, so the gap may be configuration rather than error; it is recorded as UNVERIFIABLE, not as a finding.

**Verdict: CRITICAL_ERRORS.** The method and its experimental core are mathematically sound — Eq. (3) is correctly normalised, the FLOP accounting behind Table 4 is right, and essentially every arithmetic check on the tables passes. What fails is the paper's own description of its results: three confident critical findings (the inverted FID comparison in the introduction, the abstract's FID range and “consistently outperforms” claim, and the conclusion's universal superiority claim) assert the opposite of what the tables show, and would each require correction. The nine minor findings are misreported figures that the paper's own tables contradict. Notably, in every case the tabulated data is the trustworthy artefact and the prose around it is not.

**Lean project note.** `MATH_VERIFICATION/Paper` was *reused*, not created by this run — the derived project name for any `paper.md` collides on it, and it holds a 7.4 GB shared Mathlib build. Per the skill's own deletion rule (a reused project “is not yours to remove”) and a standing instruction not to delete it, the project was kept and only the per-snippet scratch (`TMP.lean`, `claim.md`) was removed; the six proofs are archived under `MATH_VERIFICATION/Paper/Paper/Verified/Grafting5217_*.lean`.
